items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a white wooden box with louvred sides, on legs about 1.2 m above grass, that houses thermometers and a hygrometer”.
items.answer: Stevenson screen
items.markingKey: Stevenson screen: a white wooden box with louvred sides, on legs about 1.2 m above grass, that houses thermometers and a hygrometer. [1]

items.stem: Explain why the Stevenson screen has louvred sides and stands on legs about 1.2 m above grass.
items.answer: Louvres let air circulate freely while keeping out direct sun and rain; standing above grass avoids heat radiated from the ground, giving a standard air temperature.
items.markingKey: 1 mark louvres; 1 mark height/grass [2]

items.stem: Describe how a maximum-minimum thermometer is used.
items.answer: Read the bottom of each metal index: the maximum on the right-hand scale and the minimum on the left-hand scale; reset the indices with a magnet each day at the same time.
items.markingKey: 1 mark reading indices; 1 mark reset daily [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 5.1, which describes the instruments at a weather station. Instrument A is a wooden box on legs; instrument B is a cylinder with a funnel; instrument C has three spinning cups on a tall mast; instrument D is an arrow that turns on a pole; instrument E is a glass ball above a strip of card. Describe how precipitation is measured with the cylinder.
items.answer: Rain falls into the funnel and collects in a container; each day at the same time it is poured into a measuring cylinder and read in mm; then emptied.
items.markingKey: 1 mark collection; 1 mark measuring and emptying [2]

items.stem: Fig. 5.1 is a description of a school weather station. A white box with louvred sides stands on legs on the school field; a cylinder sunk into the ground has a funnel at the top; a pole 10 m high carries a set of three rotating cups and an arrow; a glass sphere sits on a stand facing south. (a) Name the instruments that measure wind speed and wind direction. (b) Describe how precipitation is measured with the cylinder.
items.answer: (a) Anemometer (rotating cups) and wind vane (arrow). (b) Rain falls into the funnel and collects in a container; each day at the same time it is poured into a measuring cylinder and read in mm; then emptied.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark collection; 1 mark measuring and emptying [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 5.1, which describes the instruments at a weather station. Instrument A is a wooden box on legs; instrument B is a cylinder with a funnel; instrument C has three spinning cups on a tall mast; instrument D is an arrow that turns on a pole; instrument E is a glass ball above a strip of card. (a) Name the instruments that measure wind speed and wind direction. (b) Explain why the anemometer is mounted on a tall mast.
items.answer: (a) Anemometer (rotating cups) and wind vane (arrow). (b) Above buildings and trees the wind is not sheltered or deflected, so readings are accurate and comparable.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “an instrument that records the highest and lowest temperatures since it was last reset”.
items.answer: Maximum-minimum thermometer
items.markingKey: Maximum-minimum thermometer: an instrument that records the highest and lowest temperatures since it was last reset. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “A thermometer should be placed in direct sunlight to measure air temperature accurately.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Direct sun heats the thermometer itself; it must be shaded in a Stevenson screen.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the day-to-day condition of the atmosphere at a place, such as temperature, precipitation and wind”.
items.answer: Weather
items.markingKey: Weather: the day-to-day condition of the atmosphere at a place, such as temperature, precipitation and wind. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between weather and climate.
items.answer: Weather is the short-term (day-to-day) state of the atmosphere; climate is the average of weather over about 30 years.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain how relief rainfall forms.
items.answer: Moist air from the sea is forced to rise over mountains; it cools as it rises, water vapour condenses to form cloud and rain falls on the windward side; air descends and warms on the leeward side, forming a rain shadow.
items.markingKey: 1 mark forced ascent; 1 mark cooling/condensation; 1 mark rain shadow [3]

items.stem: A wind rose for Colombo shows the number of days in one month on which the wind blew from each direction: N 1, NE 1, E 3, SE 3, S 1, SW 0, W 11, NW 2. There were 9 calm days. A factory is to be built on the E side of a town. Explain whether smoke from the factory is likely to affect the town.
items.answer: Rarely: the prevailing wind blows from the W towards the E, so smoke from a factory on the E side is carried away from the town.
items.markingKey: 1 mark use of prevailing wind; 1 mark judgement [2]

items.stem: A wind rose for Toronto shows the number of days in one month on which the wind blew from each direction: N 0, NE 2, E 3, SE 2, S 0, SW 0, W 9, NW 1. There were 14 calm days. (a) Check that the data total 31 days. (b) A factory is to be built on the W side of a town. Explain whether smoke from the factory is likely to affect the town.
items.answer: (a) 17 + 14 calm = 31 (b) Yes, often: the prevailing wind blows from the W, so smoke from a factory on the W side would be carried across the town.
items.markingKey: (a) 0+2+3+2+0+0+9+1 = 17; + 14 = 31 [1] (b) 1 mark use of prevailing wind; 1 mark judgement [2]

items.stem: “Relief is more important than latitude in explaining differences in rainfall between places.” Discuss this view, using named examples, and reach a supported conclusion.
items.answer: For: Windward slopes receive heavy relief rain while leeward areas lie in a rain shadow, e.g. the western Ghats compared with the Deccan plateau. Against: Latitude controls pressure belts: rising air at the Equator gives heavy convectional rain; sinking air at 20-30° creates hot deserts. Distance from the sea and ocean currents also matter. Judgement: Latitude sets the broad global pattern of rainfall, while relief explains many local differences.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Explain how convectional rainfall forms.
items.answer: The Sun heats the ground, which heats the air above; warm air rises, cools, and water vapour condenses to form cumulonimbus clouds and heavy afternoon rain.
items.markingKey: 1 mark heating and rising; 1 mark cooling/condensation [2]

items.stem: A wind rose for Toronto shows the number of days in one month on which the wind blew from each direction: N 3, NE 0, E 3, SE 1, S 12, SW 1, W 2, NW 2. There were 6 calm days. What was the prevailing wind direction?
items.answer: S

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a climate found within about 5° of the Equator with high temperatures all year, a very small annual range and heavy rainfall in all months”.
items.answer: Equatorial climate
items.markingKey: Equatorial climate: a climate found within about 5° of the Equator with high temperatures all year, a very small annual range and heavy rainfall in all months. [1]

items.stem: Explain why temperatures are high throughout the year near the Equator.
items.answer: The midday Sun is overhead or nearly overhead all year, so insolation is concentrated and passes through less atmosphere; day length is about 12 hours all year.
items.markingKey: 1 mark high Sun angle; 1 mark less atmosphere/constant day length [2]

items.stem: Explain why equatorial regions have heavy rainfall.
items.answer: Intense heating causes convection: hot, moist air rises, cools and condenses into cumulonimbus clouds; the trade winds converge at the ITCZ, forcing more air upwards; high evapotranspiration from the forest supplies moisture.
items.markingKey: 1 mark heating and rising; 1 mark condensation; 1 mark ITCZ/moisture [3]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the high angle of the Sun is the only reason for the climate of equatorial regions? Use examples you have studied. You may wish to consider: convection; evapotranspiration.
items.answer: For: The high Sun gives intense insolation and high temperatures all year, driving convection. Against: Convergence of trade winds at the ITCZ forces air to rise. High evapotranspiration from rainforests recycles moisture. Maritime air from nearby oceans adds moisture. Judgement: The Sun’s angle is the main cause, but air pressure, winds and vegetation are needed to explain the heavy, all-year rainfall.

items.stem: Describe a typical day in an equatorial climate.
items.answer: Clear, sunny morning and rising temperatures and humidity; cumulus clouds grow into cumulonimbus by midday; heavy thunderstorms in mid-afternoon; clear, warm evening.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “an area with less than 250 mm of precipitation a year and high temperatures, especially in summer”.
items.answer: Hot desert
items.markingKey: Hot desert: an area with less than 250 mm of precipitation a year and high temperatures, especially in summer. [1]

items.stem: Explain why there is very little rain in hot deserts.
items.answer: Air sinks in the subtropical high-pressure belt (the descending limb of the Hadley cell); sinking air warms and dries, so clouds cannot form; winds are often offshore and dry; some deserts are far from the sea or in rain shadows.
items.markingKey: 1 mark sinking air; 1 mark warms/no condensation; 1 mark other factor [3]

items.stem: Explain how a cold ocean current can create a coastal desert.
items.answer: The cold current cools the air above it, so the air cannot hold much moisture and is stable; fog forms over the sea but rain clouds do not develop, e.g. the Namib (Benguela current).
items.markingKey: 1 mark cools air; 1 mark stable/little moisture [2]

items.stem: Omar argues that subtropical high pressure is the most important cause of hot desert climates. How far do you agree? Give evidence for and against before reaching a judgement. You may wish to consider: Hadley cell; rain shadow; ocean currents.
items.answer: For: Most hot deserts (Sahara, Arabian, Kalahari, Australian) lie at 20-30° under sinking air. Against: Cold ocean currents cause coastal deserts such as the Atacama and Namib. Rain shadows and continentality add dryness, e.g. the Gobi (cold desert) and parts of Australia. Judgement: Subtropical high pressure is the main cause for most hot deserts, but local factors explain why some are especially dry.

items.answer: Not correct. Winters can be cool and nights cold; e.g. Riyadh averages about 15 °C in January.

items.stem: Fig. 5.3 shows air temperatures recorded over 24 hours in July at In Salah, Algeria: 03:00 20 °C, 06:00 18 °C, 09:00 23 °C, 12:00 32 °C, 15:00 35 °C, 18:00 30 °C, 21:00 22 °C, 24:00 21 °C. The sky was cloudless. Explain why the temperature range is so large.
items.answer: Cloudless skies let intense sunshine heat the bare ground by day; at night heat radiates quickly to space because there is no cloud or water vapour to trap it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark day; 1 mark night [2]

items.stem: Fig. 5.3 shows air temperatures recorded over 24 hours in July at a weather station in the Sahara: 03:00 15 °C, 06:00 13 °C, 09:00 18 °C, 12:00 26 °C, 15:00 29 °C, 18:00 24 °C, 21:00 17 °C, 24:00 16 °C. The sky was cloudless. (a) Calculate the diurnal temperature range. (b) Explain why the highest temperature occurs in the afternoon rather than at noon.
items.answer: (a) 16 °C (b) The ground keeps absorbing more heat than it loses until mid-afternoon, and heats the air above it after a delay.

items.stem: Explain how a hygrometer shows relative humidity.
items.answer: Water evaporates from the muslin on the wet bulb, cooling it; the drier the air, the more evaporation and the bigger the difference between wet and dry bulb readings; tables convert the difference into relative humidity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark evaporation cools wet bulb; 1 mark bigger difference = lower humidity [2]

items.stem: A school weather station in Dhaka recorded the following data. Mon: max 30 °C, min 20 °C, rain 12 mm. Tue: max 34 °C, min 20 °C, rain 1 mm. Wed: max 29 °C, min 15 °C, rain 3 mm. Thu: max 27 °C, min 21 °C, rain 0 mm. Fri: max 31 °C, min 25 °C, rain 6 mm. Calculate the mean maximum temperature.
“Satellites and automatic weather stations have made school weather stations unnecessary.” Discuss this view, using named examples, and reach a supported conclusion.
items.answer: For: Satellites and automatic stations give continuous, accurate data over large areas and are used for forecasts. Against: School stations teach how instruments work and how to collect and check data; they record local conditions (microclimates) that satellites miss; they are cheap. Judgement: Professional data are more accurate, but school stations remain useful for learning and for local enquiries.

items.answer: Rainfall is a total for each separate period (discrete), while temperature changes continuously.

items.answer: In low pressure air rises; as it rises it cools, water vapour condenses into cloud and precipitation forms.

items.stem: Study Fig. 5.4. Moist westerly winds cross a coastal mountain range. Station P, on the windward slopes, records 2400 mm of rain a year; station Q, 60 km away on the leeward side, records only 450 mm. (a) Explain why Q receives little rain. (b) Suggest how the type of farming might differ between P and Q.
items.answer: (a) Q is in the rain shadow: air has lost much moisture and descends the leeward side, warming, so clouds evaporate. (b) P: crops needing much rain (e.g. tea, rice) or forest; Q: drought-tolerant crops, irrigation or grazing.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark rain shadow; 1 mark descending/warming air [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “equatorial climate”?
options: The zone of low pressure near the Equator where the trade winds meet, air rises and heavy rain falls.
A tall, dark storm cloud formed by strong rising air, bringing thunderstorms and heavy rain.
A climate found within about 5° of the Equator with high temperatures all year, a very small annual range and heavy rainfall in all months.
Incoming solar radiation reaching the Earth’s surface.
items.answer: A climate found within about 5° of the Equator with high temperatures all year, a very small annual range and heavy rainfall in all months.

items.stem: Explain why there is little seasonal change in an equatorial climate.
items.answer: Sun angle and day length change very little through the year, so temperatures stay high and convection gives rain in every month.

items.answer: With no cloud cover, intense sunshine reaches the ground; the high summer Sun at about 25° latitude and long days cause very high temperatures; bare ground heats quickly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark clear skies; 1 mark summer Sun/long days [2]

items.stem: Fig. 5.2 is a climate graph for Riyadh, Saudi Arabia (25° N). Temperature (°C): Jan 14.6, Feb 17.1, Mar 21.4, Apr 26.8, May 32.4, Jun 35, Jul 36.1, Aug 35.8, Sep 32.9, Oct 27.4, Nov 20.6, Dec 15.8. Precipitation (mm): Jan 15, Feb 8, Mar 25, Apr 30, May 10, Jun 0, Jul 0, Aug 0, Sep 0, Oct 2, Nov 10, Dec 15. (a) Calculate the total annual precipitation. (b) Calculate the mean annual temperature.

Fig. 5.3 shows air temperatures recorded over 24 hours in July at Riyadh, Saudi Arabia: 03:00 11 °C, 06:00 9 °C, 09:00 16 °C, 12:00 28 °C, 15:00 31 °C, 18:00 24 °C, 21:00 14 °C, 24:00 12 °C. The sky was cloudless. Explain why the highest temperature occurs in the afternoon rather than at noon.
items.answer: The ground keeps absorbing more heat than it loses until mid-afternoon, and heats the air above it after a delay.

items.stem: Fig. 5.3 shows air temperatures recorded over 24 hours in July at Aswan, Egypt: 03:00 13 °C, 06:00 11 °C, 09:00 16 °C, 12:00 25 °C, 15:00 28 °C, 18:00 23 °C, 21:00 15 °C, 24:00 14 °C. The sky was cloudless. (a) Calculate the diurnal temperature range. (b) Explain why the temperature range is so large.
items.answer: (a) 17 °C (b) Cloudless skies let intense sunshine heat the bare ground by day; at night heat radiates quickly to space because there is no cloud or water vapour to trap it.
items.markingKey: (a) 28 − 11 = 17 °C [1] (b) 1 mark day; 1 mark night [2]

items.stem: Fig. 5.2 is a climate graph for In Salah, Algeria (27° N). Temperature (°C): Jan 13, Feb 16, Mar 20.5, Apr 25, May 30, Jun 35, Jul 37, Aug 36, Sep 32.5, Oct 26, Nov 19, Dec 14. Precipitation (mm): Jan 2, Feb 1, Mar 1, Apr 1, May 1, Jun 0, Jul 0, Aug 1, Sep 1, Oct 1, Nov 3, Dec 4. (a) Calculate the annual temperature range. (b) Calculate the total annual precipitation. (c) Calculate the mean annual temperature. (d) Explain why the place shown in Fig. 5.2 receives so little rain.
items.answer: (a) 24 °C (b) 16 mm (c) 25.3 °C (d) It lies at about 20-30° latitude under the subtropical high-pressure belt, where air sinks, warms and dries so clouds rarely form; winds are dry and offshore or it lies far from the sea.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “an instrument with rotating cups that measures wind speed”.
items.answer: Anemometer
items.markingKey: Anemometer: an instrument with rotating cups that measures wind speed. [1]

items.stem: Explain how to site a weather station so that readings are accurate.
items.answer: In an open area away from buildings and trees (which shelter instruments or cast shadows), on grass not tarmac, with instruments at standard heights; read at the same time each day.
items.markingKey: 1 mark open site; 1 mark standard surface/height/time [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 5.1, which describes the instruments at a weather station. Instrument A is a wooden box on legs; instrument B is a cylinder with a funnel; instrument C has three spinning cups on a tall mast; instrument D is an arrow that turns on a pole; instrument E is a glass ball above a strip of card. Name the instrument that measures sunshine and explain how it works.
items.answer: Sunshine recorder (Campbell-Stokes): the glass sphere focuses sunlight and burns a line on a card; the length of the burn gives hours of sunshine.
items.markingKey: 1 mark name; 1 mark how it works [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that satellites and automatic weather stations have made school weather stations unnecessary. You may wish to consider: accuracy; local conditions.
items.answer: For: Satellites and automatic stations give continuous, accurate data over large areas and are used for forecasts. Against: School stations teach how instruments work and how to collect and check data; they record local conditions (microclimates) that satellites miss; they are cheap. Judgement: Professional data are more accurate, but school stations remain useful for learning and for local enquiries.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a diagram showing how often the wind blows from each direction at a place over a period”.
items.answer: Wind rose
items.markingKey: Wind rose: a diagram showing how often the wind blows from each direction at a place over a period. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Climate can be found from one week of weather readings.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Climate is the long-term average (about 30 years); one week shows only weather.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Fig. 5.4 describes a mountain range 2500 m high running north-south. The prevailing wind blows from the west off a warm ocean. Town P lies on the western slopes at 800 m and receives 2400 mm of rain a year; town Q lies on the eastern side at 600 m and receives 450 mm a year. Suggest how the type of farming might differ between P and Q.
items.answer: P: crops needing much rain (e.g. tea, rice) or forest; Q: drought-tolerant crops, irrigation or grazing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Fig. 5.4 describes a mountain range 2500 m high running north-south. The prevailing wind blows from the west off a warm ocean. Town P lies on the western slopes at 800 m and receives 2400 mm of rain a year; town Q lies on the eastern side at 600 m and receives 450 mm a year. (a) Explain why Q receives little rain. (b) Suggest how a climate graph for Q would differ from one for P.
items.answer: (a) Q is in the rain shadow: air has lost much moisture and descends the leeward side, warming, so clouds evaporate. (b) Shorter rainfall bars in most months; possibly higher summer temperatures and a larger range because of clearer skies.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark rain shadow; 1 mark descending/warming air [2] (b) 1 mark rainfall; 1 mark temperature [2]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “insolation”?
options: Steady winds blowing from the subtropical high-pressure belts towards the Equator.
Incoming solar radiation reaching the Earth’s surface.
The zone of low pressure near the Equator where the trade winds meet, air rises and heavy rain falls.
A tall, dark storm cloud formed by strong rising air, bringing thunderstorms and heavy rain.
items.answer: Incoming solar radiation reaching the Earth’s surface.
items.markingKey: Insolation: incoming solar radiation reaching the Earth’s surface. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “The ITCZ is a zone of low pressure with rising air.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Trade winds converge, air rises and heavy convectional rain falls.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Manaus, Brazil (3° S) has an annual temperature range of 1.9 °C and 2215 mm of rain a year. In Salah, Algeria (27° N) has an annual range of 24 °C and 16 mm of rain. Compare the two climates and explain one reason for the difference in rainfall.
items.answer: Manaus, Brazil (3° S) is hot all year with a much smaller range (1.9 °C v 24 °C) and far more rain (2215 mm v 16 mm). Rising air at the ITCZ gives convectional rain at the Equator, whereas descending air in the subtropical high-pressure belt stops clouds forming in the desert.
items.markingKey: 1 mark temperature comparison with data; 1 mark rainfall comparison with data; 1 mark explanation (rising v sinking air) [3]

items.stem: Fig. 5.2 is a climate graph for Singapore (1° N). Temperature (°C): Jan 26.5, Feb 27.1, Mar 27.6, Apr 28, May 28.3, Jun 28.3, Jul 27.9, Aug 27.9, Sep 27.6, Oct 27.6, Nov 27, Dec 26.5. Precipitation (mm): Jan 240, Feb 160, Mar 180, Apr 170, May 170, Jun 140, Jul 150, Aug 150, Sep 140, Oct 160, Nov 250, Dec 290. (a) Calculate the annual temperature range. (b) Calculate the total annual precipitation.

A school weather station in Lima recorded the following data. Mon: max 31 °C, min 19 °C, rain 0 mm. Tue: max 25 °C, min 17 °C, rain 22 mm. Wed: max 30 °C, min 22 °C, rain 0 mm. Thu: max 20 °C, min 8 °C, rain 22 mm. Fri: max 19 °C, min 9 °C, rain 6 mm. Sat: max 33 °C, min 20 °C, rain 12 mm. Sun: max 22 °C, min 18 °C, rain 0 mm. (a) Calculate the total rainfall. (b) Name the instrument used to record the maximum and minimum temperatures and state where it should be kept.
items.answer: (a) 62 mm (b) A maximum-minimum (Six’s) thermometer, kept in a Stevenson screen.

items.stem: Fig. 5.2 is a climate graph for Singapore (1° N). Temperature (°C): Jan 26.5, Feb 27.1, Mar 27.6, Apr 28, May 28.3, Jun 28.3, Jul 27.9, Aug 27.9, Sep 27.6, Oct 27.6, Nov 27, Dec 26.5. Precipitation (mm): Jan 240, Feb 160, Mar 180, Apr 170, May 170, Jun 140, Jul 150, Aug 150, Sep 140, Oct 160, Nov 250, Dec 290. (a) Calculate the mean annual temperature. (b) Describe the main features of the climate shown in Fig. 5.2. (c) Explain why this place has rainfall in every month.
items.answer: (a) 27.5 °C (b) Hot all year (26.5-28.3 °C) with a very small annual range of 1.8 °C; heavy rain (2200 mm a year) with rain in every month, wettest in December. (c) High temperatures all year cause convection: hot, humid air rises, cools and condenses, giving afternoon thunderstorms; it lies near the ITCZ where trade winds converge.

items.stem: A revision website states: “All deserts are sandy.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Many are rocky or stony (reg and hamada); sand seas (ergs) cover only part of the Sahara.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why temperatures can fall below 5 °C at night in a hot desert.
items.answer: Clear skies and dry air let heat radiated from the ground escape quickly into space; there is no cloud blanket.
items.markingKey: 1 mark clear skies; 1 mark heat escapes [2]
